notes.content:
Greetings Pharaohs, 

Today, we’re glad to announce that the Mission Editor mode is now available with the latest update for Pharaoh: A New Era. Starting today, you can play the Mission Editor mode and start your kingdom from scratch to rule it in your own way. 

Disclaimer regarding map names when playing in Mission Editor mode: 

A note on map names in the new Mission Editor Mode - all of your custom maps will be shown under the "My Maps" tab in-game.

You may create additional tabs to organize your custom maps in-game by creating folders via Windows File Explorer (C:>Users>[My Windows User Name]>AppData>LocalLow>Triskell Interactive>Pharaoh>[Steam ID number]>My Maps).

However, please note that if you create two folders A and B, but each of them contains a map called "MyMap1" then you will have two maps with the same name "MyMap1" under the "My Maps" tab in-game, which may lead to confusion.

We strongly encourage you to assign unique names to your custom maps to avoid confusion in the "My Maps" tab.

notes.title: PHARAOH: A NEW ERA - NEW PATCH 1.3.0 AVAILABLE NOW
notes.content:
Greetings Pharaohs,

We’re deploying a new update that brings several QoL improvements as well as bug fixes to Pharaoh: A New Era. As always, the team is grateful to the community for its everlasting support and love for the game.

https://store.steampowered.com/app/1351080/Pharaoh_A_New_Era/

NEW OVERLAYS

NEW - Three more overlays added

 Bazar overlay - displays food access to houses
 Magistrate overlay - displays courthouses access to houses
 Problems - displays various problems in your city : 
Risk of life, collapse, crime, disease, and malaria
 No road access
 Buildings’ entry & exits that are not connected
 No access to the workforce
 No raw material available for manufactured goods production buildings
 No resources available for services buildings (i.e. mortuaries, scribal schools, libraries, senet houses, and zoos)
 Entertainers missing on performance venues

Most overlays now display information when you hover on the buildings. Furthermore, we added an option to display columns on overlays just like in the original game

EVENT MANAGEMENT

With this new update, you can now manage which events must be displayed as a notification or should be hidden. This setting can be used in a new tab in the ‘option’ menu.
Please note that requests, gifts, or invasions cannot be hidden nor displayed as notifications.

We also added a few new events :

 Population milestone
 Warning for the lack of a working dock when a water trade route is open


FLAT MODE IMPROVEMENT

Flat mode just got better with this new QoL update. Starting today, you can flatten any building with a right-click. If you right-click again the building comes up. To return to a normal view, you just have to click on the button next to the minimap or press ‘F’ (hotkey set by default).

The flat mode can now cover a good part of the needs related to map rotation. With this new addition, we believe that the mode will be more practical to use.

BURIAL GOODS

The burial goods needed are now displayed :

 In missions’ objectives
 In rating overseer
 In the information panel of monuments that requires them


FERRIES

While fixing bugs that affected ferries, something interesting occurred and we decided to keep in-game. Before, if the path of different pairs of ferries crossed, they’d stop working. After fixing this, we figured out that walkers are now able to shortcut their way to go straight to a ferry landing even if it’s not the one connected to their departure.

We think that it's a neat addition, especially for bigger cities where distance can be a problem. Anything that allows path optimization is more than welcome.

SLEEP MODE

You can now put to sleep mode all interactive buildings. Sleep mode is enabled by clicking on the Zzz button displayed in the building user interface. If you don’t want to shut down the entire industry but put to sleep mode a few buildings when lacking workers or temporarily over/underproducing certain resources, you have now a great tool to do it.

LEVEL DESIGN & MISSIONS EVENTS


 In Pyramid Scheme, the first request for Granite now triggers properly
 In Pyramid Scheme, the trade route to Dunqul Oasis now sells and buys the proper resources
 Fixed soft lock occurring in Timna (Campaign sandbox) when responding in time to the recurring Men-Nefer request
 In Henen-nesw - Sauty trade route can now reopen
 In Henen-nesw - prevents a double event after receiving a gift
 In Meidum - trade with Abu is now possible
 In On -Saqqara trade route can now reopen
 In On - the Temple Complex Building to Ra is available now
 Swapped the entry and exit point in Gateway to Atlantis
 In Rowarty - Mycenae can no longer trade right from the start. The trade route opens later.
 In Behdet - the recurring perfect flood event is now a failed flood event
 In Iunet - The Temple Complex building to Bast is now available
 In Itjtawy - Balanced the wage down/wage up events to slow down general inflation
 In Maritis - Fixed the timeline. Events now happen three years sooner.
 In Thinis - the trade route to Men-Nefer can now reopen


VARIOUS FIXES & OPTIMIZATIONS


 Added mission-type icon in campaign view when choosing a monument or a military-focused quest
 Decreased clouds size
 Fixed several things on storage to prevent stuck resources
 Removed scripted event pause option
 Workforce priorities are now properly saved
 The uncapped Zoom option is now properly saved
 Stockpiling toggle in the Overseer of Commerce is now properly saved
 The industry shuts down toggle in the Overseer of Commerce is now properly saved
 Individual resources in gifts and requests are now properly displayed (i.e. blocks of sandstone, etc.)
 Fixed overseer of commerce when stockpiling
 Fixed entertainment overlay with Bast Temple Bonus
 Reduced animation update calls
 Fix parts of events text not finding their localization
 Changed format for animations from json to binaries
 Houses now check upgrades once during the daily update
 Improved management for irrigation ditches networks
 Much more complicated optimizations implemented
 Fixed house devolution delay that used to be too long in some cases
 Fixed devolution for the modest estate when missing luxury goods
 Added festival square animation
 Fixed trade road links on the world map when cities cannot trade
 Hunters and Firefighters are now properly visible
 Fixed issue with old save and building entry and exit points
 Fixed the issue where saving a game with corrupted walkers would corrupt the save
 Fixed issue where monuments would corrupt the save
 Fixed some cases of gatherers not finding collectibles
 Pre-built monuments are no longer counted in the Monument rating
 Added new illustrations for calamity events
 Added new illustrations for some wraths and blessings
 The game now prevents unpausing using the space bar when fullscreen events are displayed
 Fixed minimap blocking click when reduced
 Drag on the minimap is now enabled
 Added commerce overseer button on the world map
 Fixed an issue where carpenters would block pyramid construction
 Added a tooltip on religious buildings that displays information on God’s moods.
 Fixed delete button displaying a smaller instance of itself on hover in the save window
 Fixed pause keybind not working after discarding some popups with a right-click or escape
 Fixed display of the Nile which was retracted by one tile
 Fixed dropdown menu displaying “empty” instead of “buy” in bazaar user interface
 Fixed title screen music that wouldn’t loop nor play again when coming back to the main menu
 Increased animation’s menu speed
 Added a quick-load button to the main menu - it will load the last save used before quitting the game

notes.title: PHARAOH: A NEW ERA - NEW PATCH 1.2.0 AVAILABLE NOW
notes.content:
Greetings Pharaohs, 

Today we finally add the long awaited ultra-wide support to the game. We also wanted to improve player experience by increasing coverage of buildings, making UI improvements and more bug fixes, most notably by fixing more save corruption issues and monuments getting stuck.


Added ultra-wide support

We could not test every variation out there, so if you encounter any problems, please provide your feedback in the Technical Support forum so we can help you.


Balancing

As the way to play the game has changed a lot in almost 24 years, neighborhoods tend to be generally more optimized than what the original team intended, generating spam of specific buildings to attain desired coverage. Coverage for buildings has been increased to reduce this:


 Shrine: from 300 to 400 people
 Temple: from 700 to 900
 Shrine for Patron God: from 150 to 200
 Temple for Patron God: From 375 to 450
 Temple Complex: from 8000 to 10000
 Juggler stage: from 400 to 600
 Musician stage: from 700 to 1000
 Dancer stage: from 1200 to 1800
 Senet House: from 5000 to 7500
 Zoo: from 7500 to 10000
 Library: from 800 to 1200
 Scribal School: from 300 to 500 children



UI&UX improvement


 Esc. now has the same effect as a right click.
 Every tooltip now gives information on what key bind is associated with its button.
 Added an icon on a building not having access to a road instead of a notification.
 Added an icon on a building whose entry and exit point are not connected.
 Mission briefing properly displays objectives in the first 4 missions.
 Objectives now display house full name instead of house level.


General Bugfix


 Trade Boats don’t get stuck when something happens to their destination dock anymore.
 Fixed Trade Boats not splitting when multiple docks are available.
 Fixed display for unit-based resources in trade boats interface.
 Walkers in destination mode no longer try to go through underwater floodplains (and drown on the way).
 Fixed some animations on buildings.
 Buildings destroyed by gods now have a lightning strike effect if you happen to be looking at the right time in the right place.
 Fixed several more cases of saves corruption.
 Fixed monuments getting stuck after loading a save.
 Fixed several other instances of monument construction getting stuck.
 Added burial tomb background in monument overseer.
 Fixed mini map not updating on certain cases.
 Fixed Academy blocking recruiters if not accessible by road when built the first time.
 Fixed tax input field not clamping the value correctly.
 Fixed trade routes opening and festival launching still sometimes not being able to be used while in debt.
 Fixed hunting lodge icon on worker overseer.
 Fixed workforce calculation for the overseer of workers.
 Disabling industries now send the workers back to being unemployed.
 Inhabitants in manors are now properly removed from the workforce.
 Fixed events on Itjtawy so new trade routes can open.
 Fixed "Organized Mess" achievement not being triggered.
 Fixed trade "Sells" column missing its border.
 Fixed city name not being updated when changing language in the settings.


Please note that in order to fix as many save corruption issues as fast as possible, we were forced to reintroduce the following bugs : 

 When loading the campaign map, improper cities are initially being shown
 Work Camps will sometimes decide to stop sending out workers | WORKAROUND : This issue occurs after around 1 hour of gameplay. Reloading the save fixes the issue.

We apologize for this inconvience, we are working to fix these bugs as fast as possible.

We want to thank you all for playing Pharaoh: A New Era. Feel free to share your feedback using Steam's Feedback & Suggestion subforum. We're doing our best to gather everything and study them carefully. 

As stated in a dev blogpost, the map editor, and military revamp are next on the list of features to come.

notes.title: PHARAOH: A NEW ERA – NEW PATCH 1.1.0 AVAILABLE NOW!
notes.content:
Greetings, Pharaohs. 

We deployed a new patch addressing some gameplay bug fixes as well as adding the highly-requested mini-map, balancing, some rework, and improvements to Pharaoh: A New Era. 

New Features:

Added mini-map to the bottom left of the screen.
Added 'Flat Mode' and 'Grid' Toggle to the mini-map. (as explained in our previous blog post, both modes already had their own key bindings: ‘F’ & ‘G’ are used by default - can be modified in the game setting)
Mini-map also displays the different food available in the mission.

 
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/cf08ca7288fb15b96c603a3d73847e430ed7c14c.jpg

Balancing:

Regrowth of trees and reeds is now calculated every month based on resources gathered and no longer total resources on the map. 
Reduced the spawn rate of animals making hunters less absurdly efficient. 
Hunters now bring back only 10 units of hides per trip, slowing down hides production.
Reduced the rate of criminal spawn - when a house generates a criminal, the crime risk of every other house is slightly reduced, avoiding waves of criminals spawning the same day and giving you time to set up police stations and courthouses.


Rework of the City Sentiment:

Added passive bonus to city sentiment each month depending on the difficulty level (+2 on easy, + 1 on normal, and no bonus on hard)
If you’re supposed to get a bonus in city sentiment this month, the bonus is doubled if the city sentiment is lower than 50% and tripled if lower than 30% - allows recovering more quickly from low city sentiment once you’ve fixed the underlying problems.
Added an alert if your city sentiment falls below certain thresholds - Below 50% immigration starts to decrease, and it stops below 30%).
Added more information regarding the city sentiment and how variables are considered in the in-game help section
Added more indications to the Chief Overseer when hovering over it - gives more precision as to why the city sentiment is falling


Rework of Religion:

Festival now gives fewer ankhs to the dedicated god (from + 3 to +2 for the Grand Festival, +2 to +1 for the lavish festival, and from +1 to nothing for the small festival).
The window for blessings after a festival is halved (16 instead of 32 months).
Festival to a god only allows for a chance to get his blessing, not other gods anymore.
General probability of getting ankhs/thunderbolts is lowered.
The threshold for blessings can only be reached after you have at least dedicated a festival to the appropriate god - preventing high mood in the early game to provide free blessings.
There is now a minimum delay of a month in between two blessings/wraths from different gods.
The same god cannot give a blessing/trigger its wrath less than 3 months apart.
You can open a trade route and throw a festival now even if you're close to going into debt. 
You can open a trade route and throw a festival now when if you're in debt
Tax rate cannot go higher than 25% any longer
Removed every mention of the tribute to the kingdom as it’s not used in A New Era - Instead, every year passing while indebted will hurt your Kingdom Rating directly.

 
UI & UX

Key binds for overseers and overlays now close what they open.
Modified the order of the overseers - reflect more what was in the original game.
There are no longer subcategories to the building bar, to avoid confusion with buildings that didn’t have one - Every building is now only two clicks away.
The chief overseer comments now have tooltips on hover which give more information.
Saves are now ordered from newest to oldest.


Added key bindings for

Undo
Remove
Housing
Road
Roadblock

 
Tutorials:

Added a tutorial in Perwadjyt to explain how entertainment coverage works.
Added a tutorial in Thinis to explain how flat mode works.
Added a tutorial in Saqqara to explain how burial provisions work.
Added a tutorial in Men-Nefer to explain how city sentiment works.
Added a tutorial in Nekhen to explain how the building picker works.
Modified the tutorial on Nubt to reflect the removal of subcategories.
Added new loading tips.

 
Options:

Added an option to toggle on/off the autosave.
Added an option to specify how many autosaves to keep for a city.
The autosave delay option now offers more choices.

notes.title: PHARAOH: A NEW ERA - GAMEPLAY OVERVIEW & USEFUL TIPS
notes.content:
Greetings Pharaohs, 

We're more than thrilled and proud to introduce a brand-new gameplay overview video of Pharaoh: A New Era. This video allows us to tackle several gameplay mechanics and introduce a few tricks to build and make your kingdom live on through the 4000 years of history narrated in-game. 

[previewyoutube=vLagi5oWyjE;full][/previewyoutube]

Pharaoh: A New Era is the remake of the beloved and original 'Pharaoh' game released in 1999. This cult classic provided an unforgettable memory to generations of players and narrated 4,000 years of the history of Ancient Egypt through six different ages. To make sure that players who have never played the original Pharaoh game feel comfortable enough we gathered some basic but useful tips to get started. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/4a8be1f1bd2875cf79c404a62718a8ba90fcfb76.png

We recommend to all beginners choose the campaign mode to get started by learning all mechanics step by step before jumping into the Free Build mode. 

Step #1: read and understand the mission briefing and the win and defeat conditions

First of all. There is nothing to worry about, whether you've already played the original Pharaoh or not.
One of the first things you absolutely need to focus on when starting to play Pharaoh: A New Era is the mission briefing that will sum up the main objectives to achieve and how to avoid defeat. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/906a8f34f47476de94f65c8dd4e4129c8af4ca8d.jpg

Step #2: Place your first plots of housing

After reading the mission briefing, it's time to start building the foundation of your dream kingdom. It all starts with the construction of plots of housing to populate the unoccupied lands of your future empire. Place the first housing to provide migrants with a suitable place to live.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/b5f8aefa304f9dcf9b804a28ff5df939b158f6ac.gif

One more tip: it's important to build roads that link the Kingdom Road to your plots of housing to guarantee access and free movement to your citizens and future workers.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/93e0f62c84b5953e57c00eac8c59db8a99a44cc1.gif

Step #3 Access to water is the key

To offer a better standard of living and upgrade your citizens' housing, it's important to place wells nearby their households in other words on lands with underlying groundwater (noticeable with grass growing on them). 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/4057b408137ffb46b595c78e8ba42c6db12db6cc.gif

Step #4: these are the services you'll need to guarantee the safety of your citizens and workers

Once the first buildings and housing are placed and water supplies are provided, it's time to build an architect's office as well as a fire station to prevent any fire or collapse. Other useful services will be available later on (police station, doctor, apothecary, courthouse, etc.).  

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/ae4f184db039a9b56e180e33c555f1bc233bc4f8.gif

One more tip: make sure to place those services nearby households and any other public building (granaries, temples, palaces, etc.). 

Step #5: local trade and exploitation of the kingdom's resources

Each kingdom has its specific layout, resources, and wildlife. To ensure good exploitation of the resources present in your kingdom it's essential to build: 


Hunting lodges to hunt the wild animals that populated the kingdom's lands and deliver the meat to the Granaries 
Granaries to preserve the meat and deliver it to distributors
Bazaar to guarantee distribution to your citizens 


{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/c671a61d8b70f6e7db056efd5431d71e7dbe613d.gif

In the next missions, you'll also have to build:


Recruitment camps near the lands that will be plowed and cultivated
Plots of chickpeas, barley, and other resources
Mine to exploit the lands that abound in precious stones such as gold
Clay pits, potteries, etc. 


One more tip: make sure to build an architect's office and fire station nearby recruitment camps, mines, or clay pits that also are also subject to fire or collapse. 

Step #6: Recruit and keep an eye on the % of unemployment

It's important to install services that require manpower in proportion to the number of working-age inhabitants. If you do not pay attention to the % of unemployment, a shortage of workers is to be expected.  

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/0270e30ba03d073220dfa27a9e1da4fb4907374b.jpg

Step #7: Make the kingdom prosper

You need to develop local trade in order to make the kingdom prosper and develop the services to improve the standard of living and well-being of your citizens. Once the kingdom will be fully industrialized, it's necessary to build a palace that will store most of the city's treasure and a tax collector's office.  

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/17c1961f8aaa726cf82cff99fb667808717a7868.gif

Step #8: Enhance the desirability rate of the kingdom:

Do your best to make your Kingdom a beautiful and peaceful place to live in for your inhabitants. Developing entertainment (juggling or dancing schools etc.), building temples and shrines in honor of the gods, or embellishing the city with gardens or ornate paving stones all contribute to the desirability of the city. Keep an eye on the rating overseer to learn more about what your citizens expect.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/7fba5ac1027474b0ef01389b4c96428bb35cca25.jpg

Step #9: Keep the Gods pleased


Each god (Bast, Ra, Osiris, etc.) has its own temple and shrine dedicated. Build them near the households to worship them. Their blessings guarantee many benefits such as a bumper crop or a remarkable abundance of raw materials. However, if they aren't worshiped enough, your city will suffer the wrath of the gods. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/b0c0870a17a4afedc567d6ce5271cde23edfa2ee.jpg

Step #10: Hold a festival in honor of the Gods

To keep the gods pleased, your citizen entertained and your kingdom more desirable, build Festival squares on a four-way intersection and hold one in honor of Bast, Osiris, Ra, or any other god that needs to be worshiped. Festivals temporarily improve the gods' mood and increase your chances of getting your kingdom blessed. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/ec86d8d298ffe3cc1cd921affbcbc670c86448b9.jpg

Louis will talk about his commitment to faithfully rearranging and enhancing the authenticity of each track from the game OST with traditional Middle Eastern instruments. He will also tell us how he managed to overcome the difficulties encountered during this beautiful and inspiring musical journey. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/a4b65bcc3c0bebd66d141c2363147338dedf2c5d.png

Hello, Louis! Let's begin this interview with a short introduction. 

Louis: Hello everyone! My name is Louis Godart and I'm a musician from Nantes - a beautiful city in the West of France that is worth paying a visit to. (he's right, you know.)

How did you start music and how did you end up working on Pharaoh: A New Era? 

Louis: I've been playing the guitar for twenty years. After playing and studying a vast array of musical genres (metal, jazz, rock, classical and improvised music) and composing for different projects, I figured out I could also work in the video game industry by joining game jams. Playing video games has always been a hobby right before I started playing the guitar (I was a huge fan of Age of Empire II in my teenage years).  

A few years later, I met Théophile Noiré (Co-founder of Triskell Interactive) and he told me he was working on the remake of a city-builder named Pharaoh. I must confess, I had never heard about it before then. 

And what can you tell about your involvement in Pharaoh: A New Era conception?

Louis: My work on Pharaoh: A New Era was pretty straightforward. I had to recreate the entire music from the original game. But you know, "straightforward" does not mean it was simple nor quick.

How did you revive the original Pharaoh soundtrack? Did you encounter any particular difficulty? 

Louis: Basically, there were four main stages to revive the Pharaoh's music. First of all, I had to transcribe the original music, in other words, use my ear to capture and gather the most important elements of each song (i.e. melody rhythm, harmony, etc.) that make them easily identifiable. The result is a simple musical skeleton with a limited number of instruments programmed in MIDI format, on which I'd later build the arrangement. 

(NB: MIDI file is a format used to connect devices that make and control sounds such as synthesizers, samplers, or computer) 

Then, I had to arrange the tracks to program virtual instruments so as to make the music sound real (and not just "the right notes with the right rhythm) when I used symphonic orchestra libraries, etc. And to be honest, this is one of the most tricky parts because this is literally the moment when the music comes alive. This is also the moment when I could take liberties with the original material (add a counter melody, use different harmony or rhythmic elements, etc.). The idea here was to absorb the music as much as possible (in other words, treat it like I had written it myself) without distorting it so players could enjoy the tracks as much as they did twenty-three years ago. 

After that, we went to a recording studio to work with musicians who play various traditional Middle Eastern instruments. Pharaoh melodies are mostly played by solo instruments so it was difficult to program expressive solo lines using my software. 

Then we finally mixed the whole soundtrack in a studio so each musical element (using virtual and real instruments) would fit into its right place and sound consistent. Arthur Lauth at Brown Bear Recording worked his magic for that matter and the result is brilliant. 

Here, you can actually listen to a comparison between different versions of sthA: 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pql9kbLQfpA

What was the biggest challenge you had to deal with when working on the game soundtrack? 

Louis: There were several challenges, to be honest, but one of the biggest was to avoid cultural appropriation as much as possible. Pharaoh: A New Era is the biggest project I ever worked on. This experience also made me understand how stressful it can be to work on a huge IP that drives so much nostalgia and expectations. The community is demanding yet extremely supportive and I really enjoyed getting to know them. 

Also, it might be surprising but the hardest thing to transcribe in Pharaoh: A New Era OST was the ambient tracks like "Agbj" "Hapj-aA" or "WATJ" since they were quite different from the rest of the soundtrack. These tracks are rather based on particular synthesizers' textures but I managed to create them with my software. 

Did you get in touch with the composers of the original Pharaoh game? 

Louis: I did! I reached out to Keith Zizza, one of the main composers, and had the opportunity to discuss some choices made in the original game (i.e. the crowd chanting in the track (jrj-Hb-sd). We also talked about the arrangements I made for the remake and it was really instructive. It was a real pleasure to exchange views with someone who worked in the video game industry back in the 90s. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/8d0b868ce4a182ac4ad0428558ece3c13eadb53b.jpg
 
How did you proceed to compose, reorchestrate and arrange everything from scratch? There were no partitions available, right?

Louis: Indeed, there was no source material left to work with. In other words, I didn't have any HD, uncompressed files, or any separate tracks whatsoever to make the transcription easier. So I had to work with the same MP3 files that can be found in the game. 

But to be honest, it wasn't that hard since ear transcription has always been a part of my musical education and I love it. However, sometimes I had some doubts regarding the kind of musical element or instrument that was used here and there. To be honest, that was literally the same kind of questioning that the graphic team had to deal with during game development (i.e. are these random pixels a clay pot or wooden box? etc.) but in my case, it was applied to music.

How long did it take to analyze the original soundtrack before starting the transcription process? 

Louis: Not that long to be honest. I just needed to listen to the whole soundtrack once or twice to get an overall idea of what needed to be done. Then I’d jump into transcription work starting with sthA which is the most famous track from Pharaoh.

How long did it take to rearrange the whole soundtrack in Pharaoh: A New Era?

Louis:Because of my self-discipline, I time-tracked my whole work on the soundtrack and I spent a total of 1000 hours working on it.

Now let's talk about Khepera, the track you'd like to introduce today. What kind of instruments were used to compose it?

Louis: Various live instruments were used to compose Khepera. When listening to it, you can hear ney, kawala, Turkish clarinet, violin, qanun, acoustic bass, and various other percussion instruments such as the daf and the rik. We also used several virtual instruments but it would take too much time to list them all. 

Listen to Khepera on my Soundcloud: https://soundcloud.com/lgodart/khepera

And how many musicians were involved? 

Louis: There were six musicians! 


 Saddam Novruzbayov: wind instruments 
 Kais Siala: violin 
 Niqolah Seeva: oud 
 Nidhal Jaoua: qanun 
 Bachir Rouimi: percussion instruments 
 Myself: acoustic bass. 


I also need to mention the excellent work of our sound engineers, Timothée Funfrock and Charlotte Davy. Their precious contribution to microphone placement helped me stay focused on the music during our recording session (there were a lot of moving microphones).

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/fa6cba48878a97457f7b8218716d04873e1a21c1.jpg

How long did it take to compose and rearrange Khepera?

I spent about: 
 

 3,5 hours to transcribe 
 12 hours to arrange 
 15 hours to record 
 5 hours to mix 

 
So I’d say a week of work at least. But don’t worry, not all the tracks needed that much time. But when it comes to Khepera, I felt the need to transcribe the spirit of the song. 

When it comes to Khepera and its rearrangement, can you tell us how you managed to keep the "authenticity" or "the spirit" of Ancient Egypt as well as the original track?

Louis: This is a tough question. The first thing I want to say is that, in terms of historical musicology, it is impossible to have a precise idea of how music sounded in Ancient Egypt. We have some clues, and we know what kind of instruments they played (i.e. kawala, sistrum) but that’s all. 

We’re talking about 5,000 years old music passed down from generation to generation through oral tradition (i.e. live performance). So, we have barely any trace of it. 

I guess the lack of trace led Keith Zizza and Henry Beckett to make some artistic choices. Overall, Pharaoh’s soundtrack reflects what Middle Eastern music is or used to be in Ancient Egypt from a Western perspective. So what I tried to do is to give the opportunity to Middle Eastern traditional musicians to play the music in their own way, which is a fair choice in my opinion. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/f3431f3671cc011dd8725a11e77b7d2bb6837e71.jpg

Louis: Middle Eastern music is extremely varied. So we tried to rely on their knowledge of Egyptian traditional music as much as we could. The result is a beautiful mix of Western and Middle Easter music. And I believe that’s also what Keith and Henry aimed for when working on Pharaoh in the 90s. 

What kind of challenges did you deal with when composing this track?

Louis: Well, while transcribing Khepera, I realized the song was written in the "key of B", which is a difficult key for some instruments. For example, the low strings ostinato in the introduction features a "low B" - a note that doesn’t exist on real contrabasses.
 
So, I decided to raise the whole song half a step up, allowing it to have a "loc C" that does exist on contrabasses and cellos - making it sound more natural and realistic when played by a symphony orchestra software. The song turned a little brighter but became easier to play for some instruments. However, I kept the song in "B" for the archaic cinematic since the arrangement was shorter. 

How would you describe Khepera? What kind of tone or feeling did you want to express with this track? 

Louis: To be honest, Khepera is one of my favorite tracks along with KHU and RA. This song is very interesting because there’s a lot of variety and different sections that tell a story from beginning to end. 

It starts with a dark and mysterious feeling, driven by that low strings ostinato, supporting a very somber, haunting flute solo (we used two different instruments for that one - ney, and kawala) that dialogues with the violin, in a nice ambiguity between "C minor" and "C hijaz" (Phrygian dominant for the music theory geeks). 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/df8a790435ffe44f0a6adc0bdfbd3a6e88d8336a.png
 
Then, after an overblown kawala effect, the whole orchestra and rhythm section begins and we dive into a melody played in unison by the oud and the qanun. Both instruments dialogue with the orchestra’s strings section. And that gives a nice contrast with the first part in regards to the timbre. 

Then there is this majestic building-up section (that has a certain progressive rock energy in it when you pay attention) with a determined palm-muted oud ostinato in unison with strings, and choirs in the background. Those heavy low hits on beat 3, supporting an expressive violin melody always raising until the ultimate earworm, the main Pharaoh theme, but played faster than in other tracks (you can hear it playing slower than in Egypt, SETUP, etc.). At this moment, it really sounds like a celebration. That’s why I decided to let the musicians play the melody as they wished, to give it a real celebration-like and spontaneous feeling. 

The end of Khepera is a long decrescendo with a violin line that sounds like a short improvisation. So I ask our violinist to play something he felt was right to conclude the track. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/69f468e529fa49fad7e26f7675cad612a6bc537e.png

Kais: Hi everyone. My name is Kais Siala and I played violin and viola on Pharaoh: A New Era’s soundtrack. At the end of Khepera, I played taksim which is a free improvisation using a certain scale or makam. In this Taksim, I used a particular makam called Hijaz Kar, which is frequently used in traditional Middle Easter music. In Western music theory, we’d call it “double harmony scale” or “Ionian flat 2 flat 5”, “byzantine" you name it… 
 
Here’s another example of a Taksim played on the out while using this makam: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b0ekco4BcuA

Louis: This is a beautiful scale! Recently, Hans Zimmer (the one and only) also used it in Dune’s (movie directed by Denis Villeneuve) original soundtrack: 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BdtiYwSP9ko

We ended up with a violin solo that was longer and different from the original version, and yet, sounded more natural. It also helped to bring the percussion loop to a natural end, instead of using a fade out. Overall, I’d say this track tells what Khepera is in Ancient Egypt mythology, a symbol of the rising sun, and the renewal of life. We start from nothing, raise to the top, and then we go back to dust before being reborn, and so on. 

I hope you will enjoy my rendition of the track as much as I enjoyed working on it!

---- 

Follow Louis Godart on Twitter: 
https://twitter.com/louisgodart 

How about checking his Soundcloud?
https://soundcloud.com/lgodart/khepera

notes.title: PHARAOH: A NEW ERA - Q&A BEHIND THE ART (PART 2/2) 🎨
notes.content:
Greetings everyone!

Today, we are back with the following (and last) part of the dev blog about the game’s Art Direction. 

First of all, we would like to apologize for the delay as this dev blog was supposed to be out last month. To be honest with you all, bad luck hit us, and part of the social team in charge was on sick leave for a while.  Anyway, we are back now, and here are some more answers from Guillaume (aka Noodle) - Art Director at Triskell Interactive! I hope you’ll enjoy reading this last part of the dev blog!

In the end, please keep in mind that every choice was made with deep respect, passion, and love for the original game.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/35822e7452cb5c1cc4a39f0cbcf47e3e8256996c.png

💬 INTERVIEW Q&A

➣ The amount of work to redesign each asset must be huge, but I imagine you also have to work on some of the sprite details, which were not necessarily there before. How do you deal with that?

Since we don't have access to the original game files, we always start working on the in-game version and scale up each asset by 2000%. It gives us a good idea of what we're working on (that's also the part when we realize that some of the details of the original game are just a bunch of pixels!). Then, we have to figure out what we are dealing with and whether this bunch of pixels is more of a carpet or a jar. Sometimes, it is even difficult to distinguish the different textures. We sometimes even wonder if we are dealing with earth, mud, or brick. So, my job is to find out what these textures are, to add details like cracks in a wall or some flowers… Also, I usually "edit" the work files, either for myself or for the team. In other words: I get the original sprite, then enlarge it and identify what might be blurry (or unclear). Finally, I put references for some objects or textures, and I establish a color chart.

Then and only then can the painting process begin. We start with the general shapes, then sharpen the details while preserving the original sprite design. It's meticulous work, but it's also a lot of fun! By using this method, we are sure to respect the spirit of the OG.


➣ What did you like best about remastering some assets? A favorite building/monument that you enjoyed (re)making? 

I enjoyed working on the monuments — especially those of the original Cleopatra extension like the Caesareum. These are Greek and Roman-inspired buildings with lots of colonnades, statues... It's tedious to do, but it stands out from the rest of the Egyptian buildings and brings a breath of fresh air to the overall look of the game. It was a very welcome (re)creative break!

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/d1d0cda12e2466a503c642e7c9b80be82c1234fa.png

➣ Do you have any particular style or inspiration in mind whenever you work on Pharaoh: A New Era?

Since Pharaoh: A New Era is all about Ancient Egypt, I have inspirations and references from historical findings and archeology. I have several books at home on the subject. IMO, Ancient Egypt is fascinating, as not a month goes by without a discovery being made. This is what makes the topic so much exciting. Otherwise, the main inspiration is the original game, of course!


➣ What were your biggest difficulties during this project?

The difficulties encountered are not necessarily due to the creation itself but rather to our choice to use isometric 2D. Many difficulties result from this choice and, sometimes, influence the way we work or even the way some assets are designed. Most of the time, we have to decompose the assets of a building, making sure those bits overlap perfectly. There are also sorting issues, i.e. sprites that are not visually on the same level as others. These are technical difficulties that we have to take into account when creating graphic assets. 

Another difficulty, which also results from the use of 2D, is the isometric perspective in the drawing process. It has many advantages but also disadvantages. Indeed, the isometric perspective is not realistic.  It is a perspective that has no vanishing point, and it is sometimes very tedious to reproduce shapes like spheres, curves, or cylinders with this perspective. We often have to cheat, but as long as the visual rendering is there, cheating is allowed.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/ab1bd54c172720b9de741367511128d83f46b2a8.png
WIP - Overseer of the Military - Placeholder text


➣ On your streams, we can see that you enjoy putting little touches of humor on the buildings. Can we expect little Easter Eggs/visuals hidden in the game?

We have always done this before at Triskell Interactive. It's more of an inside joke than anything else! In the end, we are pretty serious about our games. I don't know if there will be any Easter Eggs in the end because Pharaoh is a pretty serious game, and we have to respect that too. Pharaoh is an iconic management game and we wouldn't want players to think that we took this work lightly. We'll see!


➣ What are your best memories of Pharaoh? How does it impact your creations?

I don't know if this is my "best" memory, but I remember the game being extremely difficult. I couldn't understand why my entire city was suddenly on fire. Also, I didn't understand what some of the characters were doing. For me, the walkers were merely for show. So, the most vivid memory I have is the game's replayability. It was a long learning process, but it was very exciting. I was able to try out different setups in my neighborhoods, switch the buildings around, and see the direct effects of those changes. Once you know the game mechanics, you tend to make the same neighborhoods and arrange your cities in the same way. But at the very beginning, it's the discovery, the search for perfection, the budget balance. Those are my fondest memories of the OG.

How does that impact my creations? I'm not so sure. I think what we want to do is to make a more detailed game so that the game experience is constantly renewed. I like the player to be amazed, every time they have to restart a mission, even for the 5th time in a row. I am hoping to bring back the excitement from those younger days to the fans. That would be a great accomplishment.


➣ Since the demo and thanks to the feedback from the community, have some things changed in your way of seeing things?

Naturally, getting constructive and interesting feedback challenges our way of seeing things and our work in general. Nevertheless, we cannot possibly change everything based on all the feedback we have received (even though we do believe that feedback will always be necessary). The Art Direction is in line with the whole game and we got a lot of positive feedback about it during the demo. Unfortunately, it is sometimes necessary to distance ourselves from criticism because it can quickly become a source of anxiety for the team and can lead us to question the work we have accomplished or even make us doubt our abilities. Still, there were some aspects of the project that we were less sure of, and this allowed us to make certain decisions.

As for the game's UI, we noticed that it turned out to be frustrating for some players during the demo. So, we decided to redesign the user interface, menus, etc., to make the game experience as smooth as possible. Here’s a small example: When creating a family (profile), we have added the possibility to choose an avatar, which will allow the player to know at a glance which family is selected (on top of personifying the player in some specific sections of the UI).

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/a89dc96b1ecd41a3e71c563ff13cf95ee68d52bd.png
WIP - UI is still subject to change - Placeholder text


🦛 Love, hippos, and pyramids. 🦛

----------------------------------------------

We would also like to thank you for your feedback on the first part of the dev blog. It was a pleasure to take you all behind the scenes of Pharaoh: A New Era! In the end, we hope you’ll enjoy the game as much as we loved creating it for you.

notes.title: PHARAOH: A NEW ERA - Q&A BEHIND THE ART (PART 1/2) 🎨
notes.content:
Greetings everyone!

Today, we would like to invite you behind the scenes of Pharaoh: A New Era, with an exclusive dev blog dedicated to the game’s Art Direction. More precisely, we invite you to discover what Guillaume (aka Noodle) - Art Director at Triskell Interactive - has been working on so far.

This two-part dev blog reveals details about the creative work behind Pharaoh's graphic makeover. In this dev blog, we will also discuss the decisions made regarding the game's Art Direction, which we know is not entirely welcomed by some part of the community. Here, we are not trying to convince anyone but simply express our love and passion for the license. We fully understand that this may clash with your strong appreciation of the original game, but we hope to give you some perspective on the decisions that must be made with a production like this one. 

In the end, please keep in mind that every choice was made with deep respect, passion, and love for the original game.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/f5cde7968a8900cf90f9b5b7eb45db6ab8776bb6.png

💬 INTERVIEW Q&A

➣ So, let's start with the easy part, can you introduce yourself to the community?

I'm what we call the art director of Pharaoh: A New Era.  Basically, my main role is to make sure that all the game graphics are consistent with one another: the UI, buildings, characters, animations... I also take care of the design of the graphic assets (buildings, UI). In addition, I am the main contact between the game developers and the graphics department. I work closely with Leslie, who is also part of Triskell Interactive, also in charge of creating assets, making artworks, FX, animations, etc.


➣ What immediately comes to your mind when you think about Pharaoh?

The first thing that comes to my mind with Pharaoh is the feeling that the game is like a real living canvas. The game had left a lasting impression on me when I was young from the way it was drawn, painted, but also animated (and especially filled with great details.) To me, the game was simply amazing. Ironically, I think that's what got me into 2D / painting, even though the game was in 3D at the time. I discovered this game when I was quite young. It was one of the first PC games that my parents gave me. I must have been 13 or 14 at the time. It was the first game that introduced me to strategy games. It was very new to me because, at the time, I was mostly used to Nintendo games. However, I quickly got into it and have not stopped playing it since!

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/cb8a9f569d40a056471a8d59e99a2292c102dca0.png

➣ What do you like most about Pharaoh's spirit?

What I like most about Pharaoh is its chill/contemplative aspect. Indeed, there is something fascinating about building a neighborhood and watching it grow. You do have the impression of standing in the middle of an Egyptian city and you can see how it develops: from its birth to its fall.

Another thing I like most about the original game is the OST. Indeed, the Ancient atmosphere is further emphasized by the music. With Pharaoh: A New Era, I feel like we've been very respectful of the original work in this regard.


➣ When you are in a creative process, how do you manage to put together what you want to do artistically and what the players expect from the game?

Being a big fan of the original game helped me a lot in shaping the game's art direction. The most important thing for me was to respect the original game and its artists, as the original game was incredible visually. Indeed, they managed to find the perfect balance between the game's visual aspect and its gameplay. I wanted to keep this particular balance. As for the painting and the 2D style, it is, for me, the real spirit of the game. I wanted to respect it as much as possible for the players.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/b1018cc602a6446368bab223bb006f78cdbad5c7.png

➣ When you first started working on Pharaoh, what were the main aspects of the game that you were looking to improve and develop, and what were the ones you wanted to keep from the classic games?

In my opinion, there were a few things that didn't feel right in the original game that I wanted to improve. For example, the shiny, body-built characters looked outdated, as did the game's UI originally designed for 4:3 aspect ratio resolutions. The game was released in 1999, so graphics standards have evolved a lot, as well as computer hardware.

I didn't want Pharaoh: A New Era to be a mere graphical redesign. So, we tried to modernize the graphics while respecting the original artists' work as much as possible. Somewhat like an archeologist, my job is to dust off the old sprites, making them brighter, more fitting to today's standards. As for the aspects that I absolutely wanted to keep, well, it's precisely this "living canvas" aspect that impressed me so much, as well as the depth of detail. In this regard, using 2D, i.e. digital painting, seems ideal to me. I think we made the right choice in using this technique.


➣ In the end, how do you manage to respect the original spirit of the game, while making it "more modern"?

Well, finding the right balance can be very tricky. For example, we used the sprites from the original game to create the new building designs. Still, at the same time, we try to modernize them and improve on what has already been done. It includes a subtle change of colors to make the game brighter, the addition of animations and visual effects: a bird flying by, dust escaping from a collapsing building. Also, today's screen resolutions allow us to go into more detail: a few random pixels in the original game can become a clay pot in Pharaoh: A New Era, and I think that's our magic trick.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/b77d6c17b79bdb12e6c2ad9b8fb92cc2cc3680f5.png

➣ What would you have to say to those fans who don't necessarily like the cartoon aspect of Pharaoh: A New Era?

We knew from the very beginning that we would have to make choices. These choices could not please everyone and it was a dilemma that we had to accept from the start to move forward.

Since we didn't have the original game's resources, and we had to redo everything, we decided to fully focus on the 2D aspect (walkers included). It brings more harmony between the buildings and the characters' design. Of course, some former players are fond of the "realistic" look of the original game, especially with the walkers. However, while I was working on Pharaoh: A New Era, I decided to change some of the walkers' details that I thought were overly caricatural (e.g the bodybuilder look and their shiny bronze skin). So we decided to distance ourselves from this aspect and turn to something closer to our sensibility: the cartoon style. Pharaoh: A New Era also needed to be adapted to today’s standards. The game was already gorgeous in 1999, and I understand that some fans still find it gorgeous, myself included! However, the idea of making this remake was to modernize its visual aspect. So we chose to keep the original design of the buildings (using digital painting) and to remake the walkers so they would be more noticeable, more detailed, and more adapted to the artistic direction of the project.

- Love, hippos, and pyramids. 🦛

notes.title: ASK ANYTHING TO CHRIS BEATRICE - ANSWERS Part.2
notes.content:
Greetings everyone, 

In this first part, you will find below all questions and answers related to the following topics: 


 Improvements and what if
 Other topics


{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/2781db01f3f864f6f89f8079cf6ac0bba774dd9f.png

Naalnish (Discord):

Q:  If there was one thing you could improve on in the original Pharaoh game what would it be and why?

Chris: Well, if I had to choose one thing, I would deal with combat better. Either get rid of it or make it smooth and fun (which, it’s safe to say, it isn’t in the original game). 

At the time RTS games were just coming into their own, and it was hard to gauge how the game would be received if it didn’t have any combat, or what standard the combat would be held to by players. We didn’t have enough time to make it really great, but we felt we needed to give players some influence over the result of combat encounters. I just remember having no bandwidth to deal with it properly, because with a development schedule that tight you need to stay focused on the core of the game, which was the city-building...


Other questions: What compromises did you and your team make to achieve a good balance between historical accuracy and gameplay? 

Looking back on Pharaoh and Cleopatra, is there anything that you think of now that you wished you and the team had done differently? 

Are there any features/gameplay elements that you wanted to include but had to be cut due to technological limitations at the time? Again, thank you for the AMA, and thank you for Pharaoh, it is honestly my favorite game of all time.

Chris: 1. Compromises, well, they’re all over the place, but I don’t really look at it that way. Having currency, markets delivering food to houses, even the idea of a planned city is alien to the setting. What made many of these choices easy was the fact that we had the underlying Caesar III gameplay as both an asset and a limitation. 

One thing that could have been a compromise but we made work was the fact that the pyramids, including the great pyramid at Giza, which are probably the most well-known and recognized monuments in the world, considered the height of the Egyptian civilization, came very early in the history of Egypt. It would have worked better for them to be more like the end goal in the campaign, but the historical timeline was one area where I wanted to stick close to reality...

2. I had nothing to do with Cleopatra, really. As for Pharaoh, you know, I guess, I’d have to say, no. Because nothing is perfect, and given the time and resources we had, to have made a  game that people still talk about, well, I couldn’t ask for more. I guess I’d say that I wish after the success of Pharaoh I’d focused the studio entirely on the city-building games. But at the time it was kind of taboo for a studio to only do one thing.

3. Thanks for the kind words about Pharaoh. It’s wonderful to have been part of something that has touched so many people and continues to inspire. As far as gameplay elements, as I said in response to someone else, I really wish we’d done a better job with combat, either made it really good (though simple), or just not included it, and handled it with auto-calc (and maybe some more advanced troop-creation options)

And I always wished we’d been able to polish the game more. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38626053/5f7934455942fb510fdb6208f02c240ffd826f49.png

Fro (Discord):

Q: Do you still have hope that Medieval Mayor will be developed and released one day? What was the idea behind the local work pool? More realism? But why did you decide then that a couple of houses are sufficient to have access to all workers on the map? Is that a feature you’d have made differently afterward? 

Chris: I do want to make Medieval Mayor! Like a lot of creators, I have too many projects I want to do. 

PC gaming and gaming in general have gone through a lot of big changes between Pharaoh and now. Now, it seems, everyone is a gamer, which is GREAT. There is room for lots of different games. The main reason I keep holding off on Medieval Mayor is I don’t feel confident I could provide enough security for the team making it. 

When Sierra and I parted in 2001 my goal was not to make great games or express myself creatively--it was to make a company that would provide great jobs for the people who worked there. Honestly, that is more of what I was always about when making games. But the two go together, more than people might realize. A lot of great bands making great music fall apart because they can’t work together, you know? So I wanted to make a company that was sustainable and a great place to work, with creators from all different disciplines working well together, being listened to, etc. That was TMill. 

When I set up Tilted Mill and was asking people to trust me enough to quit their full-time jobs to join our team, I needed to know that I could provide enough stability to make that work out for the long term. But things are different today, and it’s hard to sustain a large team indefinitely. At least I don’t feel confident enough that I could guarantee that level of security. Of course, some former colleagues are telling me not to worry about that, but…

Red Maw (Discord) 

Q: What are you playing right now? What games have impressed you the most lately? 

Chris: I’ve been playing Trine (1, 3, and 4) on Switch, and also Nine Parchments. Plus lighter games like Mario Cart just for fun. Honestly I never really played hardcore games much because playing them is in a lot of ways similar to making them, I always felt. Problem-solving, focusing for hours, etc., I’d always find myself stopping and switching back to designing. So when I play now it’s about a light, fun, co-op experience (with my kid).

Fro (Discord)

Q: Had you ever imagined your games would be played for decades?

Chris: No! It’s one reason I was not eager to get into making games, actually. If you write a great book, people will be reading it a hundred years later. But because games are so tech-dependent, they don’t age well, however successful they might be at the time. So we have franchises that last decades, but no so many individual games. In this sense, Pharaoh has greatly exceeded my expectations, and I still miss working with that team.

Jolanser (Discord) 

Q: After Impressions made the city-builder series, Tilted Mill went on and made Children of the Nile which has many different systems (pull walkers instead of push walkers, the economic system, the difference in social classes). Are there any of these systems or mechanisms in Children of the Nile you would have wanted to back-port into Pharaoh or the other games in the city-builder series?

Chris: That’s a really insightful question/point! Yes, I do think all the time about how the different systems work and how they might be combined for better gameplay.
I’ve done a few designs over the years and always found myself merging the good aspects of the two approaches that you identified so accurately. The push system is great for moving around a lot of resources without a lot of “walkers”--the advantage there being the visual communication to the player of what is happening. But the downside, obviously, is the non-sensical outcome where a house says it’s lacking something even though it’s right around the corner. In these cases, a targeted pull system works. 

VAIA (Discord):

Q: If you had infinite resources available and you were making Pharaoh 2, what would you add or change?

Chris: Honestly, I would spend a lot more time and money on a lot of things that are invisible, vs. being explicit features or other content. That means playtesting and polishing, fixing, or getting rid of what’s not working until the game is truly seamless and near perfect. But that was not the model we used back in those days. I would resist the urge to make it more realistic (either visually or in terms of historical accuracy) and make it a smoother experience that was easier for beginners to get into.  

AmenusUK (Steam) 

Q: Your msg site tiltedmill appears to be broken. is it gone for good?
2- Can you tell us how many units of Caesar3, CaesarIV, Pharoah, Emperor have sold worldwide to date?
To conclude I love all these games and so looking forward to the new Pharaoh coming out.

Chris: Whoops, uh, yeah, I’ll get Jeff Fiske right on that.
2. I think it was more than four million overall, but I may be way off by now.

Tearfrom the red (STEAM)

Q: Hi Chris, if you could make a successor to the game using any civilization at any time in history, what would you pick?

Chris: Medieval Europe! I like this setting because it was a time of great technological development, and also feels kind of quasi-fantasy, like ancient Egypt. And the castles provide a similar opportunity as monument building. I’m not sure how / if I’d integrate combat, though.

Lucas_Amorim (Steam)

Hi Chris! First of all, thank you to provide me one of the best experiences that I already had in the 00's pc games. You're like Sr. Myiagi for me when I speak of game developers.

Q: How you made to searching and studying about the old Egypt civilization? Did you talk to historians? Buy some books? Attended museums?

Chris: Thank you so much for the kind words.
For research, it was lots and lots of books, on top of many years already spent studying. I watched whatever videos I could find as well. This was basically pre-internet. I still have most of the books I bought for Pharaoh. I bought them with my personal money so I could hang onto them.

Navin Kumar 

Q: Why did they choose so few of the Egyptian gods for temples? Unlike Zeus

Chris: The short answer is: Because Pharaoh was about the monuments whereas Zeus was about the gods.

With games, unlike other forms of entertainment, it’s vital that players are already somewhat familiar with the “rules of the setting” so to speak. Whether it’s fantasy or sci-fi or history, this is true, because as an interactive media, the player is not simply receiving—they are also participating. If they make a decision based on experience or intuition and it does not produce something like the effect they imagine, it’s no fun. It’s frustrating or even infuriating. So if I’m playing a fantasy game I expect the rogue character to be good at shooting stuff, for example. Any attempt at a clever twist on that runs the risk of ruining the player’s experience. To put a positive spin on this principle, by using that rogue character you, the designer, are capitalizing on the player’s prior experiences. Then you need only stoke the fun, not make it entirely from nothing.

Most people are very familiar with the Greek and Roman gods.  In fact, to many people “ancient Greece” and “mythology” are synonymous. If you ask someone to name a few, and what they represent, they will be able to do that. But not so much with the Egyptian gods. We are talking entirely about popular understanding here, of course.  With Egypt, “what it’s about” is the pyramids. 

So it’s a question of focus. Pharaoh would have worked fine with more gods, but then they’d have been more nuanced, the lines between them even less clear, on top of the fact that they are unfamiliar to most people.
